reasons: Both answers are written in English to a Russian-speaking user, translate the discharge wording (keeping the Russian only in parentheses) and open with an English boilerplate disclaimer, so both fail the language requirement. Both explain NYHA II correctly and avoid calling it end-stage, but both misdescribe the Strazhesko-Vasilenko stages: B rebuilds them as an exertion-level scale (IIB = mild activity, III = symptoms at rest), and A says IIA means symptoms only on exertion. B's plan reflects current quadruple therapy and its analogy is plainer, which offsets A's slightly smaller staging error.

A: Describes stage IIA as symptoms only on exertion with the heart coping at rest; in Strazhesko-Vasilenko, IIA means hemodynamic disturbance (congestion) in one circulation that is present at rest
B: Redefines Strazhesko-Vasilenko stages by exertion level (IIA moderate, IIB mild activity, III symptoms at rest); IIB actually means pronounced disturbance in both circulations and III is terminal with irreversible organ changes
Stage I described as heart damaged but no symptoms on normal activity; Strazhesko stage I is latent failure with symptoms only on exertion
